q: What is a convolutional layer?
short: A layer that slides learned k×k×C_in filters over the input, computing a weighted sum at each position to produce one feature map per filter.
detail: Local connectivity and weight sharing; parameters (k²C_in + 1)C_out independent of image size.
mistakes: Saying each position has its own weights.

q: Why do CNNs work well on images?
short: Images have local, repeated, hierarchical structure; CNNs exploit it with local receptive fields, shared filters (translation equivariance) and stacked layers that compose features.
detail: Far fewer parameters than dense networks, so they generalise better.
follow: When would a CNN be a poor fit?
mistakes: Claiming CNNs are fully rotation invariant.

q: Output size of a 32×32 input, 5×5 kernel, padding 2, stride 1?
detail: General formula ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1.
follow: What padding keeps size for k = 7?

q: Max pooling vs average pooling?
short: Max keeps the strongest activation per window (most common, robust detection); average keeps the mean (smoother; used as global average pooling at the end).
detail: Both parameter-free; max backprops only to the arg-max.
follow: Why replace pooling with strided convs?

q: What is padding and why use it?
short: Adding zeros around the input so the output keeps its size and border pixels contribute; 'same' padding p = (k − 1)/2 for stride 1.
detail: Valid = no padding; full = k − 1.

q: What is a receptive field?
short: The region of the input that can influence a given neuron; it grows with depth, kernel size, stride and pooling.
detail: Stacked 3×3 stride-1: 3, 5, 7, 9.
mistakes: Confusing kernel size with receptive field.

q: What does a 1×1 convolution do?
short: Mixes channels at each pixel (a per-pixel dense layer): reduces or expands channel count and adds non-linearity cheaply.
detail: Core of NiN, Inception bottlenecks, ResNet, MobileNet.
follow: Compute the savings of a bottleneck.

q: What is a residual (skip) connection?
short: The block outputs F(x) + x, so it only learns a correction; the identity path keeps gradients flowing in very deep networks.
detail: Projection (1×1 stride 2) when shapes differ.
follow: Why did plain deep networks fail?
mistakes: Calling it a fix for overfitting.

q: What is transfer learning?
short: Starting from a network pre-trained on a large dataset (ImageNet) and adapting it: freeze and train a new head (feature extraction) or fine-tune with a small learning rate.
detail: Choice depends on data size and similarity.
example: 2,000 dog photos → freeze ResNet, train classifier.
mistakes: Fine-tuning with a large learning rate.

q: Why do CNNs typically use ReLU?
short: Cheap, non-saturating for positive inputs (gradient 1), sparse activations; helped AlexNet train deep CNNs fast.
detail: Dying ReLU is the main risk; Leaky ReLU/GELU alternatives.
follow: What is the dying ReLU problem?

q: Parameters of a conv layer: 3×3 kernels, 128 input channels, 256 filters, with bias?
detail: Independent of the 56×56 spatial size.
follow: How many multiply-adds for a 56×56 output?

q: Derive the gradient of the loss w.r.t. a conv kernel.
short: ∂L/∂K(m, n) = Σ_{i,j} ∂L/∂Out(i, j) · In(i + m, j + n): a cross-correlation of the input with the upstream gradient; ∂L/∂b = Σ ∂L/∂Out.
detail: Input gradient = full convolution of upstream gradient with the flipped kernel.
example: Shared weights sum contributions from all positions.
follow: How does stride change the backward pass?
mistakes: Treating each position's kernel as separate parameters.

q: Compute the 1×1 bottleneck savings for a 5×5 conv 256 → 256 via 64 channels.
detail: The slide's 147,456 / 11× is an arithmetic slip.

q: Strided vs dilated convolution?
short: Strided downsamples (smaller output, larger RF) — classification backbones. Dilated keeps resolution and enlarges RF with gaps — segmentation, WaveNet. Same parameters.
detail: Dilation risks gridding artefacts.

q: Why stack 3×3 convs instead of using a 7×7?
short: Three 3×3 layers have the same 7×7 RF with 27C² vs 49C² weights and two extra non-linearities.
detail: VGG's key idea.

q: What is global average pooling and why replace FC layers with it?
short: Average each channel to one value (H×W×C → C); no parameters, input-size flexible, less overfitting; the last conv channels act as class evidence maps.
detail: 7×7×512 → 1000 classes: 25.1M (flatten+FC) vs 513K (GAP+FC).
follow: How does GAP enable class activation maps?

q: Your CNN reaches 99% train but 70% validation accuracy. What do you try?
short: Overfitting: data augmentation, dropout, weight decay, smaller model or GAP head, early stopping, transfer learning from a pre-trained backbone.
detail: Check data leakage and distribution shift too.

q: Write a NumPy 2-D cross-correlation (valid, stride s).
short: o = (n − k)//s + 1; out[i, j] = sum(I[i*s:i*s+k, j*s:j*s+k] * K).
detail: Vectorise with im2col for speed.
example: Code ex1 reproduces the slides' feature maps.
follow: How does im2col turn this into a matrix multiply?

q: Why did deeper plain networks have higher training error, and how does ResNet fix it?
short: An optimisation problem, not overfitting: deep stacks struggle to represent identity and suffer degraded gradients. Residual blocks make identity the default (F = 0) and add a gradient term of 1 through each block.
detail: ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y (1 + ∂F/∂x); ensemble-of-paths view; BN helps too.

q: Multiply count of Inception 3a's 3×3 and 5×5 paths with and without 1×1 reductions.
detail: Slides: 390M vs 118M.
mistakes: Forgetting the reduction layers' own cost.

q: Are CNNs translation invariant?
short: Convolutions are translation equivariant; invariance comes approximately from pooling/GAP. Strides and pooling cause aliasing, so small shifts can change outputs.
detail: Anti-aliased pooling (blur before subsample) improves shift robustness.
example: Classifier flips prediction after a 1-pixel shift.

q: Design a CNN for a phone app classifying 20 plant species with 5,000 images.
short: Pre-trained efficient backbone (MobileNet/EfficientNet-B0), replace head with GAP + dense(20), freeze then fine-tune later blocks with small η, heavy augmentation, class-balanced sampling, quantise for mobile.
detail: Validate on photos from different users/devices.
example: Feature extraction first, then selective fine-tuning.
follow: How would you handle a new species later?

q: Depth vs width vs resolution scaling?
short: Depth adds hierarchy and RF (harder to train); width adds features per layer (quadratic parameter growth, easy to parallelise); resolution adds detail (quadratic compute). EfficientNet scales all three with α·β²·γ² ≈ 2.
detail: Wide ResNets can match deeper ones.

q: Compute cost of a conv layer and how to reduce it.
short: ≈ H′·W′·k²·C_in·C_out multiply-adds. Reduce via 1×1 bottlenecks, depthwise-separable convs (k²C_in + C_inC_out per pixel), fewer channels, lower resolution, factorised kernels.
detail: Depthwise separable ≈ 8–9× cheaper for 3×3 (MobileNet).
